headline: Claims the Thorp shuffle on 2^d cards randomizes the whole deck in order d shuffles, the best possible order.
scope: The Thorp shuffle on decks of 2^d cards, measured by total-variation distance of the full permutation from uniform, from any starting deck.
plain: The Thorp shuffle cuts a deck in half and interleaves the two halves, with a coin flip deciding the order of each matched pair. With 2^d cards, each single card is spread out after d shuffles. The papers claim the whole deck is close to random after 1600d shuffles, and at least about 2d are needed. So the right number is a constant times d. Lean proofs check the main mixing theorem and many supporting estimates.
doesNot: This does not find the exact leading constant or a sharp cutoff. It does not cover decks whose size is not a power of two.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Ben Morris, the first bound polynomial in d via evolving sets
scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles the order of the mixing time for a well-studied shuffle with uses in cryptography.

explanation:
Take 8 cards, so d = 3. Cut the deck into two halves of 4. Pair the first card of each half, then the second cards, and so on. For each pair, flip a fair coin to decide which card goes first. Then lay the pairs down in order. That is one Thorp shuffle. Each shuffle uses 4 coin flips, so 3 shuffles give at most 2¹² = 4,096 different orders. But there are 8! = 40,320 orders of 8 cards. So after 3 shuffles, the deck is still far from random, even though each single card is now equally likely to be anywhere. An exact computer count gives a distance from uniform of about 0.898 after 3 shuffles. It falls to about 0.20 after 5 shuffles and 0.026 after 8.

That distance is total variation. It is half the summed gap between the shuffled deck's probabilities and the perfectly random ones. The general lower bound is 1 − 2^(tn/2)/n! after t shuffles of n cards[1]. For n = 8 and t = 3 it gives 1 − 4,096/40,320, about 0.898, matching the exact count. The mixing time is the first t where the distance is at most 1/4. The bound says this takes about 2d − O(1) shuffles at least.

Thorp introduced the shuffle in 1973[2]. For 2^d cards, Morris got the first bound polynomial in d, of order d⁴⁴[3]. Montenegro and Tetali improved it to d²⁹, and Morris later to d³[4,5]. The obstacle is that single cards mix fast, but the joint order of all n cards holds far more information.

The main paper claims 1600d shuffles bring the whole deck close to random as d grows, from any starting deck[6]. With the lower bound, the mixing time is a constant times d[1]. The constant 1600 is a convenient choice, not a sharp one[7]. The proof labels positions by binary strings, the corners of a cube[8]. It tracks most cards one at a time, then recovers the rest with Fourier analysis on the group of all orders. Companion papers claim other routes to the same order. One gives 512d shuffles[9]. Another reaches distance ½n⁻⁵ after a fixed number of full sweeps[10]. A third uses a new inequality for 4-by-4 permanents[11].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof of the main theorem. After 1600d shuffles the distance tends to zero, from every starting deck. Lean also covers the trace-smoothing bound and many supporting estimates, including the four-row permanent inequality. Several papers' full conclusions sit outside their selected Lean statements. No specialist review of these papers has been published.
hypeCheck: The headline mixing theorem has a Lean proof. It settles the order, not the exact constant. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: Cut the deck in half, pair matching positions, flip a coin for each pair's order, and interleave.
Half the sum, over all orders of the deck, of the gap between their actual and perfectly random probabilities.
The number of shuffles needed before the deck is within distance 1/4 of uniformly random.
Every order of the deck is equally likely.
Breaking a probability law on permutations into pieces, one for each basic symmetry pattern, and bounding each piece.
Like a determinant of a square matrix, but every term is added with a plus sign.
